query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Removal of Co from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy shifts the balance of dislocation‐mediated plasticity toward enhanced, dynamically activated twinning (via a reduced or altered stacking fault energy) such that at higher strain rates and elevated temperatures the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy maintains its strength–ductility balance by increasing work‐hardening through twin formation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase solid solution high-entropy alloy with a composition derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by eliminating Co (yielding a FeNiCrMn alloy).
generation.intervention: Perform controlled tensile (or compressive) deformation tests over a range of strain rates (from quasi-static ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ up to dynamic ~10³ s⁻¹) and temperatures (from room temperature up to ~773 K), with microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD, or in situ high-speed imaging) to quantify dislocation versus twin activities.
generation.conditions: Testing within the regime of room temperature to ~773 K and strain rates spanning 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 10³ s⁻¹ in a chemically inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, ensuring that dynamic effects are isolated.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced activation of deformation twins (and associated dislocation re-organization) acting as barriers that increase work hardening.
generation.mechanism: The absence of Co modifies the stacking fault energy and solute/dislocation interactions so that, under dynamic loading (high strain rates and moderate-to-elevated temperatures), there is a shift from pure dislocation glide to a combined twinning-assisted plasticity. This dynamic twin activation accommodates plastic strain, maintaining ductility while also providing additional barriers to dislocation motion (thus enhancing strength).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline, the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy should display an increased strain hardening rate and higher twin density under high strain rate and elevated temperature conditions, preserving or even improving the strength–ductility balance despite dynamic softening.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with its established dislocation-mediated and twin-mediated deformation behavior.
generation.boundary: Applicable within the experimental regime of temperatures from approximately 293 K to 773 K and strain rates from ~10⁻³ to 10³ s⁻¹; outside this regime (e.g., extreme cryogenic or ultra-high temperature conditions) the mechanism may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative shifts in deformation mode (from dislocation glide to increased twinning) are expected based on compositional modification, the exact quantitative change in twin density and work hardening rate remains uncertain and requires experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline. Subject both sets to identical tensile tests across the defined temperature (293 K to 773 K) and strain rate (10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 10³ s⁻¹) conditions in an inert atmosphere. Use in situ digital image correlation and post-mortem TEM/EBSD analysis to quantify twin density and work hardening behavior.
measurements: Stress-strain curves to extract yield strength and strain hardening rates
Quantitative assessment of twin versus dislocation density from TEM/EBSD imaging
Comparison of dynamic strain rate sensitivity between the two alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in twin density or work hardening rate relative to the Co-containing baseline under identical dynamic conditions (i.e., no observable shift in deformation mode), then the hypothesis—that the removal of Co leads to enhanced twinning-induced work hardening—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). AbstractMedium-entropy alloys (MEAs) have attracted considerable attention in recent decades due to their exceptional material properties and design flexibility. In this study, lightweight and non-equiatomic MEAs with low density (~5 g/cm3), high strength (yield strength: 1200 MPa), and high ductility (plastic deformation: ≧10%) were explored. We fine-tuned a previously developed Ti-rich MEA by microalloying it with small amounts of Ni (reducing the atomic radius and increasing the elastic modulus) through solid solution strengthening to achieve a series of MEAs with enhanced mechanical properties. Among the prepared MEAs, Ti65Ni1 and Ti65Ni3 exhibited optimal properties in terms of the balance between strength and ductility. Furthermore, the Ti65Ni3 MEA was subjected to thermo-mechanical treatment (TMT) followed by cold rolling 70% (CR70) and cold rolling 85% (CR85). Subsequently, the processed samples were rapidly annealed at 743 °C, 770 °C, 817 °C, and 889 °C at a heating rate of 15 °C/s.
